title: Back-rank mates

D0.outcome: Explains why a king behind its own unmoved pawns can be mated on its first rank by a single rook or queen check.

D1.outcome: When told 'find the back-rank mate', finds it, including with a preceding capture or exchange that removes a guard.

D2.outcome: In mixed sets, finds the back-rank mate for either side, and spots when his own back rank is the weakness, with no theme named.

D3.outcome: Counts the defenders of the back rank, finds the exchange or deflection that removes the last one, and decides whether to make air for the king now or later.

misconceptions: Making air for the king (a luft) early is always wise.
A back-rank mate needs a rook; a queen or two minor pieces can finish too.
sources: sources/sheets/nimzowitsch_my-system.md §4 ideas 7, 21 (queen checks on the eighth; exchanges that win by back-rank mate)
sources/sheets/edlasker_chess-strategy.md §4 K6 (d), K17 (b) (a luft is correct once a mate threat shows, not before)
conditions: The king is boxed by its own pawns with no flight square and no piece guards the first rank.
The checking piece cannot be captured, and the check cannot be blocked.
A series of exchanges can remove the last guard and end in the mate.
contrasts: The defender has a flight square, an interposition or a guarding rook, so the 'mate' is only a check.
Making a luft as a precaution long before a mate threat exists costs time and loosens the king's cover.
A castled king with a luft already open or a pawn moved is not subject to this mate.

soft_prereq_notes.FND.CASTLE.D1: castling is how the king gets boxed in
